a.explanation: Six days after chemotherapy the patient is neutropenic (leukocyte count 100/mm3 with 5% neutrophils) and febrile — febrile neutropenia. Filgrastim (G-CSF) stimulates granulocyte production and is the appropriate pharmacotherapy to raise the leukocyte count. Leucovorin rescues methotrexate toxicity, dexamethasone is an antiemetic/steroid, and interferon alfa has antiviral/immunomodulatory roles.

Progressive numbness and weakness of hands/feet (symmetric peripheral neuropathy) after chemotherapy is classic vincristine-induced peripheral neuropathy (microtubule inhibitor → axonal damage). Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis, cyclophosphamide causes haemorrhagic cystitis, and doxorubicin causes cardiotoxicity.

A nonselective beta-blocker eyedrop (timolol) can be absorbed systemically and precipitate bronchospasm in a smoker/COPD/asthmatic — worsening shortness of breath. Apraclonidine (alpha-2 agonist), epinephrine and latanoprost (prostaglandin analogue) do not cause bronchospasm.

a.answer: Explain the adverse effects this herbal supplement has on the patient's treatment
a.explanation: Madagascar periwinkle contains vinca alkaloids (vincristine/vinblastine). The herbal supplement adds to the patient's chemotherapy (vincristine) — potentiating myelosuppression and neurotoxicity. The correct response is to explain the supplement's adverse interaction with his treatment. Asking him to stop outright or continuing silently is incomplete; multivitamins don't address the interaction.

Trastuzumab (anti-HER2/neu monoclonal antibody) is used for HER2-overexpressing breast cancer and is well known to cause cardiotoxicity — congestive heart failure (reversible cardiomyopathy). Bevacizumab causes hypertension/bleeding, imatinib causes oedema/hepatotoxicity, rituximab causes infusion reactions.

SERMs (raloxifene, tamoxifen) increase the risk of venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE) — the major warning when prescribing raloxifene. They do not increase infections, severe N+V, or secondary leukaemia (that is more associated with alkylators/topoisomerase II inhibitors).

A plant product that 'enhances' (stabilizes) tubulin polymerization and inhibits depolymerisation, causing mitotic arrest, is a taxane — paclitaxel. Vincristine/vinblastine do the opposite (inhibit tubulin polymerisation). Etoposide and topotecan are topoisomerase inhibitors.

Leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue is given to protect normal cells from high-dose methotrexate toxicity (DHFR inhibition). In osteosarcoma neoadjuvant therapy (doxorubicin + cisplatin + high-dose methotrexate), leucovorin rescues normal tissues from methotrexate.

Paclitaxel (taxane) adjuvant therapy causes dose-limiting peripheral neuropathy (and alopecia, myelosuppression) — in addition to alopecia and nausea/vomiting. Heart failure is doxorubicin's hallmark; haemorrhagic cystitis is cyclophosphamide's; nephrotoxicity is cisplatin's.

Multidrug resistance to multiple chemotherapeutic drugs is most commonly caused by increased efflux via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) — pumping drugs out of the cell. Amplification of target/metabolizing enzymes and increased DNA repair cause narrower, single-agent resistance.

Adriamycin (doxorubicin) in ABVD (and MOPP's derivatives) causes cumulative dose-dependent cardiomyopathy leading to CHF years later. Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis; dacarbazine and prednisone are not cardiotoxic.

Shortness of breath in an ABVD-treated patient suggests bleomycin pulmonary toxicity (pneumonitis/fibrosis) — a hallmark dose-limiting effect. Doxorubicin causes cardiac toxicity, vinblastine neuropathy, dacarbazine myelosuppression/N+V.

CML is driven by the BCR-ABL fusion (Philadelphia chromosome). Imatinib, a BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is the standard targeted therapy. Busulphan, cyclophosphamide and trastuzumab are not first-line for CML.

Leucovorin rescue 'releases' the block of methotrexate by providing reduced folate — the efficacy of methotrexate against cancer is increased when combined with leucovorin rescue in high-dose regimens (protects normal cells, allowing higher MTX doses).

Bleomycin chelates iron and generates free radicals that cause DNA strand breaks — intercalation with iron-dependent radical formation is its mechanism. Doxorubicin also intercalates but its signature is topoisomerase II inhibition + free radicals; the iron/strand-break description fits bleomycin best.

Latanoprost (prostaglandin F2α analogue) is used topically once daily for open-angle glaucoma (increases uveoscleral outflow). Pilocarpine is a miotic used multiple times daily; tropicamide is a mydriatic; carteolol is a beta-blocker used twice daily.

Nivolumab (anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor) in melanoma commonly causes immune-related vitiligo (melanocyte destruction). Ipilimumab causes colitis/dermatitis; vemurafenib (BRAF) causes rash/photosensitivity; trametinib (MEK) causes rash.

Tropicamide (antimuscarinic mydriatic/cycloplegic) causes blurred near vision and photophobia. To reverse the mydriasis the ophthalmologist would use pilocarpine (muscarinic agonist miotic). Phenylephrine is an alpha-agonist mydriatic used in fundoscopy — of the options, the one used in funduscopic examination (dilating) is phenylephrine.

Palmar psoriasis (thick skin) responds best to a potent topical corticosteroid such as betamethasone valerate. Hydrocortisone 1% is too weak for palms; oral prednisolone risks rebound pustular psoriasis; emollients alone are insufficient.
Cisplatin is a highly emetogenic chemotherapeutic (requires prophylactic NK1/5-HT3 + dexamethasone). Vincristine, chlorambucil and 6-mercaptopurine are low–moderate emetogenic.

Cyclophosphamide is a prodrug activated by hepatic cytochrome P-450 (CYP2B6/3A4) to phosphoramide mustard (active alkylating species). 5-FU, doxorubicin and methotrexate are not P-450-activated prodrugs.
Chlorambucil, a nitrogen-mustard alkylating agent, preferentially targets lymphoid tissue — it is used in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and lymphomas. Myeloid tissue is more affected by busulphan.

Procarbazine inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase and causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (flushing, tachycardia, nausea). It is part of the MOPP regimen. Dacarbazine, melphalan and hydroxyurea do not cause this.

A plant alkaloid (Catharanthus roseus) causing peripheral neuropathy, significant alopecia and minimal myelosuppression is vincristine. Vinblastine causes more myelosuppression and less neuropathy; cytarabine and etoposide are not plant alkaloids.

Doxorubicin (anthracycline) acts by multiple mechanisms: DNA intercalation, topoisomerase II inhibition (blocking DNA synthesis and causing strand breaks), and free-radical generation. It is the classic multi-mechanism anthracycline.
Bevacizumab is a monoclonal antibody against VEGF-A that inhibits tumour angiogenesis. Anastrozole and exemestane are aromatase inhibitors; imatinib is a kinase inhibitor.

Telomerase is the enzyme that maintains telomere length, allowing cells to escape replicative senescence — a target in cancer therapy. Aromatase synthesises oestrogen, CD20 is a B-cell marker, topoisomerase unwinds DNA.

Imatinib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor of BCR-ABL) is now preferred for chronic myeloid leukaemia. Busulphan is an older alkylating agent; the question asks for the alkylating agent 'preferred for CML' — historically busulphan was used, but with imatinib listed, imatinib is the correct modern answer for CML management.

Myelosuppression (bone marrow depression) is the dose-limiting major toxicity of alkylating agents (nitrogen mustards, busulphan, cyclophosphamide). Alopecia occurs but is not the major dose-limiting toxicity.

Resistance to 6-MP and 6-TG (purine antimetabolites) most commonly results from decreased HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase) activity, since these prodrugs require HGPRT activation to nucleotides. Increased DHFR causes MTX resistance; efflux causes MDR resistance.

Fluorouracil (5-FU) is used systemically for adenocarcinomas (colon, breast, gastric) and topically for skin cancers (actinic keratosis, basal cell); it inhibits thymidylate synthase and DNA synthesis. Cytarabine is for leukaemia; vinblastine and cladribine are not used topically for skin cancer.

Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that inactivates 6-mercaptopurine — co-administration causes excessive 6-MP toxicity (myelosuppression). Thioguanine is inactivated differently (not by XO to the same degree); therefore mercaptopurine is the classic interaction.

Vinca alkaloids (vinblastine, vincristine) bind tubulin and inhibit polymerisation → depolymerization of microtubules and mitotic arrest. Azatadine is an antihistamine; cladribine and methotrexate are antimetabolites.

Topotecan is a topoisomerase I inhibitor used in metastatic ovarian cancer; its dose-limiting toxicities are neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. Vincristine, doxorubicin and mitomycin are not topoisomerase I inhibitors with this indication.
Etoposide is a topoisomerase II inhibitor active in the late S–G2 phase of the cell cycle. Topotecan is topoisomerase I; vincristine and paclitaxel are microtubule agents.

Irinotecan is a prodrug activated to SN-38, a topoisomerase I inhibitor used in fluorouracil-nonresponsive colon cancer; its dose-limiting toxicity is delayed diarrhoea (plus myelosuppression). Vincristine, paclitaxel and docetaxel are microtubule agents.

Daunorubicin is the anthracycline whose major clinical use is in acute leukaemias (AML/ALL). Doxorubicin is used for solid tumours/lymphomas; dactinomycin for Wilms/EWing sarcoma; bleomycin for lymphomas/testicular.

a.answer: D. Ameliorate cystitis caused by them
a.explanation: Mesna binds and inactivates acrolein (the urotoxic metabolite of cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide) in the urinary tract, preventing haemorrhagic cystitis. It does not potentiate cytotoxicity, retard excretion, or block emesis.

Mitomycin is an antibiotic anticancer drug bioactivated (by reductive activation) to an alkylating agent; it is selectively toxic to hypoxic solid-tumour cells. Doxorubicin, vincristine and plicamycin do not fit this description.

Idarubicin is an anthracycline analogue used in acute myeloid leukaemia, often combined with cytarabine (ARA-C); cardiotoxicity (congestive heart failure) can occur in combination. Plicamycin, bleomycin and paclitaxel are not anthracyclines.

Plicamycin (mithramycin) inhibits osteoclasts and lowers serum calcium — used in hypercalcaemia of malignancy (independent of antitumour action). Dactinomycin, doxorubicin and bleomycin do not have this calciotropic action.

Colon cancer is relatively chemoresistant, while choriocarcinoma and testicular cancer are highly curable with chemo; diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is also chemo-sensitive. Colon cancer (solid, relatively resistant) is the answer.

a.answer: Drugs more beneficial if major toxicities are non-overlapping
a.explanation: A key dosing principle of combination chemotherapy: combine drugs with non-overlapping toxicities so full doses of each can be given, maximising tumour kill while limiting side effects. Low-dose frequent administration, infrequent dosing and 'rarely effective in combination' are incorrect.
Melphalan, chlorambucil and cyclophosphamide are all nitrogen-mustard alkylating agents that can be administered orally — hence 'All of the choices'.

Streptozocin (nitrosourea) is selectively toxic to pancreatic islet beta cells — used for insulin-secreting islet cell carcinomas (and sometimes carcinoid/NHL). Busulfan, cyclophosphamide and thiotepa do not share this selectivity.
Cisplatin is given with bleomycin and vinblastine (BEP regimen) for non-seminomatous testicular cancer. Dacarbazine, procarbazine and altretamine are not part of this regimen.

Cisplatin causes severe acute (and delayed) nausea and vomiting — highly emetogenic, requiring aggressive antiemetic prophylaxis. Renal dysfunction and ototoxicity are significant but the major ACUTE side effect is N+V.
Purine antagonists cause rapid tumour lysis → hyperuricaemia → nephrotoxicity and gout. Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) is co-administered to prevent uric acid nephropathy and gouty attacks.

Carboplatin's dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia), unlike cisplatin whose dose-limiting toxicity is nephrotoxicity. Hepatotoxicity and cardiotoxicity are not dose-limiting for carboplatin.

Oxaliplatin causes dose-limiting peripheral neurotoxicity (acute cold-induced dysaesthesia and chronic neuropathy). Cisplatin's dose-limiting toxicity is nephrotoxicity/ototoxicity; carboplatin's is myelosuppression.

Cytarabine (ara-C) is used primarily for acute leukaemias (AML, ALL) and high-grade lymphomas — NOT non-small-cell lung cancer. NSCLC is treated with other agents (platinum doublets, taxanes, targeted therapy).
5-Fluorouracil is used for head and neck cancer, hepatocellular cancer, and anal cancer — so 'All of the choices' is correct.

Gemcitabine is a pyrimidine antimetabolite used primarily for pancreatic cancer, non-small-cell lung cancer, bladder cancer and breast cancer. Hodgkin's lymphoma and soft tissue sarcoma are not primary uses.
Dactinomycin commonly causes diarrhoea, mucosal ulceration and glossitis (GI mucositis) — so 'All of the choices' is correct.

Clobetasone butyrate (e.g., 0.05%) is a very potent (Class I) topical corticosteroid — more potent than clobetasone propionate, hydrocortisone, or mometasone furoate ointment (potent but not the most potent). Note: clobetasol propionate would be the strongest; among the options clobetasone butyrate is the most potent.

Pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia) is best treated topically with selenium sulphide shampoo (or ketoconazole shampoo) applied to affected skin. Permethrin is for scabies/lice, benzyl benzoate for scabies, amphotericin B IV for systemic fungal infection.

Imiquimod (immune response modifier) is used for actinic keratosis, basal cell carcinoma and genital warts — NOT for eczema. Urea cream, tacrolimus ointment (calcineurin inhibitor) and betamethasone cream are all used in eczema.

Pegaptanib is an anti-VEGF aptamer (monoclonal-type RNA aptamer) used intravitreally for wet macular degeneration. Bevacizumab is used off-label for AMD; of the options, pegaptanib is the agent specifically approved and described as an aptamer/monoclonal-type for macular degeneration.

Bacitracin ointment is applied topically to the eyelid margin for blepharitis. Trifluridine is an antiviral for herpetic keratitis (not topical on skin); ciprofloxacin and natamycin are eye drops for bacterial/fungal keratitis.

Recurrent urticaria is best managed with a non-sedating H1 antihistamine (loratadine) as first-line. Montelukast is add-on for chronic urticaria, oral prednisolone only for severe flares, and topical steroids are not useful for urticaria.

b.modelAnswer:
a) THREE CLASSES OF DRUGS FOR PRIMARY OPEN-ANGLE GLAUCOMA WITH EXAMPLES (3 marks):
1. Prostaglandin analogues — latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost (increase uveoscleral outflow).
2. Beta-blockers — timolol, carteolol, betaxolol (decrease aqueous humour production).
3. Alpha-2 adrenergic agonists — brimonidine, apraclonidine (decrease aqueous production + increase uveoscleral outflow).
(Also acceptable: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors — dorzolamide, brinzolamide; miotics/parasympathomimetics — pilocarpine; or a combination.)
b) MODE OF ACTION OF THE ABOVE DRUGS (6 marks):
- Prostaglandin analogues: bind FP receptors on the ciliary body → relax ciliary muscle and remodel extracellular matrix → increase uveoscleral (alternate) outflow of aqueous humour → lower intraocular pressure (IOP).
- Beta-blockers (timolol): block beta-1/beta-2 adrenoceptors on the non-pigmented ciliary epithelium → reduce cyclic AMP → decrease aqueous humour formation (by ~20–30%) → lower IOP.
- Alpha-2 agonists (brimonidine): stimulate prejunctional alpha-2 receptors → reduce aqueous production and enhance uveoscleral outflow; also have a neuroprotective effect.
- Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (if given): inhibit carbonic anhydrase in ciliary epithelium → reduce bicarbonate and aqueous formation.
- Miotics (pilocarpine): stimulate muscarinic receptors → ciliary muscle contraction → pull on scleral spur → open trabecular meshwork → increase conventional outflow.

a) TWO CLASSES OF KINASE INHIBITORS WITH EXAMPLES (2 marks):
1. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) — imatinib (BCR-ABL), erlotinib/gefitinib (EGFR), sunitinib/sorafenib (VEGFR/PDGFR), lapatinib (HER2/EGFR).
2. Serine/threonine kinase inhibitors — vemurafenib (BRAF), trametinib (MEK), everolimus/temsirolimus (mTOR kinase).
b) TWO CLINICAL APPLICATIONS OF EACH (4 marks):
- Imatinib: chronic myeloid leukaemia (BCR-ABL); GIST (KIT/PDGFRα-positive gastrointestinal stromal tumours); also Ph+ ALL.
- Erlotinib/gefitinib: EGFR-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer; pancreatic cancer (erlotinib).
- Sunitinib/sorafenib: renal cell carcinoma; hepatocellular carcinoma (sorafenib); GIST (sunitinib second-line).
- Vemurafenib: BRAF V600E-mutant melanoma; hairy-cell leukaemia (off-label).
- Everolimus: advanced renal cell carcinoma; everolimus-eluting stents / tuberous sclerosis; neuroendocrine tumours.

TWO TOPICAL DRUGS FOR ACNE AND MODE OF ACTION (5 marks):
1. Benzoyl peroxide (2.5–10% gel/cream): releases free-radical oxygen → oxidises and kills Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes; also mild comedolytic and reduces inflammation. Used alone or with antibiotics/clindamycin.
2. Topical retinoid — tretinoin (adapalene, isotretinoin gel): binds retinoic-acid receptors → normalises follicular keratinisation → prevents microcomedone formation and reduces comedones; anti-inflammatory.
3. Topical antibiotic — clindamycin (1% lotion/gel): inhibits bacterial protein synthesis (50S ribosome) → reduces C. acnes colonisation and inflammatory lesions; usually combined with benzoyl peroxide to reduce resistance.
4. Azelaic acid (15–20%): inhibits bacterial protein synthesis and reduces keratinisation; useful in acne with hyperpigmentation.
(Answer two with mechanism — e.g., benzoyl peroxide + clindamycin, or adapalene + benzoyl peroxide.)

c.modelAnswer:
CHOPP IN NON-HODGKIN'S LYMPHOMA:
a) DRUGS REPRESENTED BY CHOPP (4 marks):
C = Cyclophosphamide
H = Hydroxydaunorubicin (Doxorubicin, Adriamycin)
O = Oncovin (Vincristine)
P = Prednisone (prednisolone)
P = Procarbazine
(Note: classic regimens are CHOP [without the second P] or C-MOPP; the question's CHOPP adds procarbazine — credit the five letters as written.)
b) MODE OF ACTION OF EACH DRUG (8 marks):
- Cyclophosphamide: nitrogen-mustard alkylating agent; hepatic P-450 activation to phosphoramide mustard → alkylates/cross-links DNA (N7 of guanine) → blocks DNA replication → cell death (cell-cycle non-specific).
- Doxorubicin (hydroxydaunorubicin): anthracycline antibiotic — intercalates between DNA base pairs and inhibits topoisomerase II → DNA strand breaks; also generates free radicals via iron-dependent redox cycling → DNA/membrane damage; inhibits DNA/RNA synthesis.
- Vincristine (oncovin): vinca alkaloid — binds beta-tubulin and inhibits microtubule polymerisation → metaphase arrest (M-phase specific); disrupts mitotic spindle.
- Prednisone: glucocorticoid — binds cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor → modulates gene transcription; induces apoptosis in lymphoid cells (lympholytic); anti-inflammatory and anti-lymphoma effect.
- Procarbazine: methylhydrazine derivative — activated to a methyl-diazonium cation that methylates/alkylates DNA; inhibits DNA, RNA and protein synthesis; also a MAO inhibitor (hence dietary/tyramine and alcohol cautions).
c) TWO SIDE EFFECTS OF EACH DRUG (8 marks):
- Cyclophosphamide: haemorrhagic cystitis (acrolein metabolite — prevent with hydration + mesna); myelosuppression (leukopenia); alopecia; SIADH; secondary malignancy (bladder).
- Doxorubicin: dose-dependent cardiotoxicity (cardiomyopathy/CHF — cumulative >450–550 mg/m2); myelosuppression; mucositis/stomatitis; alopecia; red urine.
- Vincristine: peripheral neuropathy (areflexia, paraesthesia, foot drop); constipation/ileus (autonomic neuropathy); alopecia; SIADH; (spares marrow).
- Prednisone: hyperglycaemia; immunosuppression/infection; Cushing's features (weight gain, moon face); osteoporosis; GI ulceration; mood changes; adrenal suppression.
- Procarbazine: myelosuppression; N+V; disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol; MAO-inhibitor interactions (hypertensive crisis with tyramine); CNS depression.
